question_text: Find the order and degree of the differential equation x^(1/2)(d²y/dx²)^(1/3) + x·dy/dx + y = 0.

mark_split.label: Cube both sides to remove the fractional power

insider_note: The fractional power sits on the highest derivative alone, so it is cleared by cubing the WHOLE equation, not by touching the x·dy/dx + y terms that already sit outside the bracket.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Cube both sides to remove the fractional power
steps.margin_note: One mark. Isolate the bracket with the fractional power, then cube both sides to clear it.
steps.memory_tip: A cube-root exponent 1/3 clears by cubing both sides — the standard reciprocal-power move.
steps.why: Isolating the bracket that carries the fractional power before cubing keeps the algebra clean, and cubing both sides removes the 1/3 power exactly.
common_mistakes: Cubing the individual terms x^(1/2) and (d²y/dx²)^(1/3) separately instead of the whole isolated bracket.
Forgetting to cube the right-hand side (x·dy/dx + y) as well, leaving a mismatched equation.

steps.label: State the order and degree
steps.margin_note: The last mark. After cubing, d²y/dx² appears to the power 1 alone — that exponent is the degree.
steps.memory_tip: Once every fractional power is cleared, degree is simply the exponent sitting on the highest-order derivative.
lines: The highest order derivative present is d²y/dx²,
The exponent of d²y/dx² in the cleared
steps.why: With the fractional power removed, the cleared equation is a polynomial in the derivatives, so order and degree can be read directly from the highest-order term d²y/dx², which appears only to the first power.
common_mistakes: Reading the degree from the cubed right-hand side (x·dy/dx + y)³ instead of from the left-hand highest-order derivative.
Stating degree = 3 by copying the cubing power instead of checking what power d²y/dx² itself carries after cubing.
